\title{Selection Beats Compression: Memory Decision\\Policies for LLM Agents Under a Bounded Store}

\maketitle

\begin{abstract}
Agents built on large language models (LLMs) accumulate conversations far
longer than any context window, so a memory layer must decide what to keep,
compress, forget and recall. Existing memory systems are evaluated end to end,
so the value of each of these decisions on its own is unknown. We present
MemGate, a harness that sits between an agent and a frozen LLM, isolates the
memory policy, and compares policies on a common accuracy-per-token frontier,
changing one factor at a time. Every interval is a paired bootstrap clustered
by conversation, and the primary metric, answer recall, checks that the answer
text itself reaches the context rather than only the identifier of its turn.
We first show that the usual accounting, which bounds the assembled context
but not the store, charges a store-everything baseline nothing for retention.
Once the store is bounded, choosing which turns to forget gains $+9.37$
answer-recall points over oldest-first eviction at identical storage, fidelity
and retrieval on LoCoMo (95\% CI $[+5.45, +14.90]$), whereas compressing
evicted turns instead of dropping them loses $7.13$ points, with no
rate--distortion crossover up to $182\times$ compression. A 1.5B model that
rewrites evicted turns narrows this gap but does not close it. Counting the
embedding index in the budget reverses the ranking below about 40\,KiB. An
LLM judge of salience loses to a regular-expression heuristic by $5.87$
points, because salience is not a property of a turn read on its own. A
logistic scorer over shallow features and a sentence embedding, trained on
generated and human conversations together, beats the heuristic by $+14.55$
points on held-out conversations. It transfers from human to generated
dialogue but not the reverse, and outperforms MemGPT-style and Mem0-style
memory at every budget tested. On held-out chats of up to ten million tokens
it beats retrieval on every corpus. When million-token chats are typed into
the application it keeps the answer for 51.9\% of questions against 19.2\%,
and through a fixed reader $+6.0$ points of its advantage become correct
answers. The
learned scorer ships in an offline chat application built on the
experimental code.
\end{abstract}

\begin{IEEEkeywords}
large language models, agent memory, context management, retrieval-augmented
generation, rate--distortion, empirical evaluation
\end{IEEEkeywords}
